reader: AI reader 7 (targeted check at the stated place, PDF)

results.corrected_extracted: 278 people with methamphetamine dependence were assessed in four one-month periods (baseline, 3 months, 1 year, 3 years); all were interviewed at the first three time points and 230 (83%) at 3 years, giving 1064 person-months. Psychotic symptoms were present in 25% of observed months (273 months in the Table), and 60% of participants had symptoms in at least one observed month.
results.corrected_locator: Method › Participants and procedure (p. 320); Results › Characteristics of the sample, 3rd paragraph (p. 321); Table, column 'Yes (n=273 mo)' (p. 322)
results.note: Checked printed pp. 320–322. The 278 participants, four time points and 1064 months are on p. 320, but only 230 of 278 (83%) had the 3-year interview (278×3 + 230 = 1064), so not every person was observed in four windows; 25% and 60% are on p. 321, while the 273-month count appears only in the Table on p. 322 (273/1064 = 25.7%, which the text gives as 25%).

Checked Results › Relationship between psychotic symptoms and methamphetamine use, 1st paragraph (printed p. 321): OR 5.3 (95% CI 3.4–8.3), P < .001, after adjusting for 16 or more days of alcohol and/or cannabis use (model 2); the abstract on p. 319 repeats it. Every number matches, so only the page is added.

Checked the Table (printed p. 322): for 1–15 d and 16–28 d the unadjusted ORs are 4.8 and 15.8, model 1 (all drugs entered together) 4.2 (2.5–7.3) and 12.0 (5.8–25.1), and model 2 (only factors linked to psychotic symptoms) 4.0 (2.5–6.5) and 11.2 (5.9–21.1). Every number matches, so only the page is added.

results.corrected_locator: Results › Relationship between psychotic symptoms and methamphetamine use, 2nd paragraph (p. 321); Figure (p. 322)
results.note: The 2nd paragraph of the Relationship subsection (printed p. 321) gives 7% and 48% from model 2, and the Figure (p. 322) shows 7 and 48 in the group with fewer than 16 days of cannabis or alcohol use. In the PDF this paragraph comes before the Table, not after it; the 48% applies to that low cannabis and alcohol group (61–69% with frequent cannabis and/or alcohol use).

Checked the last Results paragraph before Comment (printed p. 321): ORs 2.25 (95% CI 1.29–3.90) for 1–15 days and 3.90 (1.80–8.45) for 16 or more days versus abstinence after also adjusting for the listed factors; numbers and factor list match. The paper does not use the word 'attenuated': the authors say these factors could not account for the association, with both estimates still significant (P = .004; P < .001).

results.corrected_extracted: Days of methamphetamine use were self-reported; hair analysis in a subsample of 83 people from the wider cohort found false reporting of abstinence in 6% of cases. Psychotic symptoms were rated by trained interviewers (agreement 93%, kappa 0.86, in 42 audiotaped interviews rated by a second interviewer); the paper does not state whether interviewers were blind to methamphetamine use.
results.note: Checked Method › Measures on printed p. 320: days of use were self-reported (Opiate Treatment Index) and the hair-analysis check covered 83 people from the wider cohort, with false reporting of abstinence in 6%. The paper does not say that symptoms were rated by the same interviewer or that interviewers were unblinded, so that part is an inference to be marked as the editors' appraisal, not attributed to the paper.

results.corrected_locator: Comment, 7th paragraph (starts 'Although the fixed-effects analysis'; direction of causality) and 8th paragraph (starts 'The outcomes from our study'; people with methamphetamine dependence), counting paragraphs in the printed PDF
results.note: Both statements are on printed p. 323: the fixed-effects analysis does not indicate the direction of causality, and the findings apply to people with methamphetamine dependence and should not be generalized to people who use stimulants recreationally or to the general population. Counting Comment paragraphs in the PDF these are the 7th and 8th, not the 6th and 7th; the authors add that for methamphetamine the direction of effect is supported by case reports, experimental induction of symptoms and the dose-response finding.

Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph (printed p. 321) gives use in 58% of months, median 8 days (range 1–28) and injection as main route (79%, vs 14% smoking and 6% snorting or swallowing), all within the sentence about months of methamphetamine use. The count 612 is not printed but equals the Table cells for 1–15 d plus 16–28 d (429 + 183 = 612 of 1064, p. 322; 57.5%, given as 58% in the text).
